items.title: What Silent Spring changed
items.claim: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring was published in 1962. Which US policy outcome is widely traced to its influence?

options.text: Founding of the US EPA in 1970 and the 1972 DDT ban

items.reveal_title: EPA founded 1970; DDT banned for agricultural use 1972
items.reveal:
Carson's book linked DDT and other synthetic pesticides to ecological damage. The chemical industry attacked the book; the EPA was nonetheless founded under Nixon in 1970.

DDT remains permitted under the Stockholm Convention for disease vector control.
items.why: Single works of science writing have sometimes redirected national environmental policy.

items.title: Why the Montreal Protocol worked
items.claim: The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out ozone-depleting substances. By the early 2020s what is the projected outcome?

options.text: The ozone layer is on track to recover to 1980 levels around mid-century outside the polar regions
The hole has expanded since the protocol

items.reveal:
WMO/UNEP scientific assessments (2018 and 2022) report stratospheric chlorine peaking in the late 1990s and recovery to 1980 ozone levels by around 2040 outside polar regions; 2066 over Antarctica.

Unreported CFC-11 emissions detected in 2018 were largely addressed by 2021.
items.why: A small group of carefully targeted treaties has produced large measurable atmospheric outcomes.

items.title: Paris Agreement targets
items.claim: The Paris Agreement (2015) commits parties to holding warming below 2 C and pursuing efforts to limit it to what?
items.reveal:
Article 2 of the Paris Agreement specifies 'well below 2 C' and 'pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 C'. IPCC's 2018 SR15 report assessed the 1.5 C pathway in detail.

In 2023 the global mean temperature anomaly briefly exceeded 1.5 C above pre-industrial.
items.why: Climate policy numbers carry technical meaning beyond their headline use.

items.title: Planetary boundaries
items.claim: The 2023 update to the planetary boundaries framework (Richardson et al.) found how many of the nine boundaries had been transgressed?
items.reveal_title: Six boundaries transgressed in the 2023 assessment
items.reveal:
Richardson et al. (2023, Science Advances) reported climate change, biosphere integrity, biogeochemical flows, land-system change, freshwater change and novel entities all outside the proposed safe operating space.

Ozone, ocean acidification and atmospheric aerosol loading remained within their limits.
items.why: Environmental science increasingly operates with multi-dimensional dashboards rather than a single climate metric.

items.title: Living Planet Index decline
items.claim: The WWF/ZSL Living Planet Report 2022 reported the average size of monitored vertebrate populations had changed by how much since 1970?

options.text: Declined by an average of around 69%

items.reveal_title: An average 69% decline in monitored populations
items.reveal:
The LPI is a population-weighted average, sensitive to extreme declines in subsets. Critics (e.g. Leung et al., 2020) note skewed samples; the headline figure should be read alongside the methodology.

Freshwater populations showed the steepest declines.
items.why: Indicators that combine many populations can be both informative and easily misread.

items.title: IPCC AR6 on attribution
items.claim: IPCC AR6 Working Group I (2021) concluded what about the cause of observed warming since around 1850?

options.text: It is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land

items.reveal:
The AR6 WGI Summary for Policymakers (2021) used 'unequivocal' for the first time in IPCC headline statements.

The assessment also tightened estimates of climate sensitivity to a likely range of 2.5-4 C per CO2 doubling.
items.why: IPCC's calibrated language tracks evolving confidence as evidence accumulates.

items.title: How much plastic enters the ocean
items.claim: Jambeck et al. (2015, Science) estimated annual plastic input to the oceans from coastal countries. What was the order of magnitude?

options.text: A few hundred tonnes per year
Roughly 4.8-12.7 million tonnes per year (2010 estimate)

items.reveal:
Jambeck et al. (2015) estimated 4.8-12.7 million metric tonnes for 2010. Later estimates (e.g. Borrelle et al., 2020) project rises absent intervention.

The known sinks (surface, beach, deep sea, biota) account for only a fraction of the modelled input, leading to active debate on missing plastic.
items.why: Pollution accounting often produces estimates with wide uncertainty bands but striking headline numbers.

items.title: Amazon dieback risk
items.claim: Research from the early 2020s suggests parts of the Amazon may be approaching a tipping point at what threshold of deforestation?
items.reveal:
Lovejoy and Nobre (2018) proposed a tipping point of 20-25% deforestation, combined with climate change, beyond which large parts of the Amazon could shift to savanna.

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon stood near 17% by 2020 by INPE measurements.
items.why: Ecosystem tipping points have policy salience even when their exact value is uncertain.

items.title: Ocean pH change since pre-industrial
items.claim: Surface ocean pH has fallen since the late 18th century. By approximately how much?

options.text: About 0.1 units (around 30% rise in hydrogen ion concentration)

items.reveal:
Mean surface ocean pH has declined from around 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times. The pH scale is logarithmic, so this is roughly a 26-30% rise in hydrogen ion concentration.

The IPCC SROCC (2019) projected further decline of 0.3-0.4 by 2100 under high-emission scenarios.
items.why: Small numbers on a log scale can correspond to large biological consequences.

items.title: Solar cost decline
items.claim: Utility-scale solar PV levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) fell by roughly how much between 2010 and 2022?
items.reveal:
IRENA's 2023 cost report found utility-scale solar PV LCOE fell from around $0.45/kWh in 2010 to $0.049/kWh in 2022 in real terms.

Wind and battery costs followed similar trajectories.
items.why: Technology learning curves can outpace policy timelines on energy transition.

items.title: Yellowstone wolves: the headline vs the evidence
items.claim: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995. The story of dramatic 'rivers changing course' from a trophic cascade has been widely shared. What does subsequent research say?

options.text: The full headline cascade is well supported in all sites
Effects on elk, willows and beavers are real but more localised and partial than the viral story implies

items.reveal_title: Real effects, less dramatic than the viral version
items.reveal:
Marshall et al. (2013) and later work found vegetation responses were patchy and depended on hydrology and other carnivores. The strongest behavioural-cascade claims have been challenged.

The ecological story remains genuinely interesting; the simplified version travels further than the nuanced one.
items.why: Popular ecological narratives often outrun the evidence even when the underlying science is robust.

items.title: Methane's GWP comparison
items.claim: Methane is a more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 over short timescales. Approximately how does its 100-year global warming potential compare?

options.text: Around 28-30 times CO2 over 100 years (IPCC AR6)

items.reveal_title: About 28-30x over 100 years; closer to 80x over 20 years
items.reveal:
IPCC AR6 reports GWP-100 of around 27-30 for fossil and biogenic methane. Methane's atmospheric lifetime is about 12 years, making it a strong near-term lever.

The Global Methane Pledge (2021) targets a 30% cut by 2030.
items.why: Choice of GWP averaging window shapes how big methane appears to be as a problem.
